domainContent.title: NoSQL Databases & Distributed Storage Engines

spark.summary: Adopting Cassandra, DynamoDB, or MongoDB while modeling tables like normalized SQL schemas creates hot-partition throttling, tombstone read timeouts, and brittle application-side joins. Engineering high-scale NoSQL systems requires query-driven partition-key modeling, bounded time-bucketed partitions, LSM-Tree compaction discipline, and tunable quorum consistency (`R + W > N`).
spark.keyTakeaway: When designing storage tiers on NoSQL engines, model partition and clustering keys directly around bounded high-QPS query paths with composite time buckets so writes append sequentially to LSM MemTables without hot-shard throttling or tombstone scan timeouts.
spark.byteSummary:
NoSQL engines trade multi-table SQL joins and cross-partition ACID transactions for predictable single-digit millisecond latency and horizontal shared-nothing scale.

Across Key-Value (DynamoDB), Document (MongoDB/Cosmos DB), and Wide-Column LSM stores (Cassandra/ScyllaDB), physical data placement is governed by the **partition key**. A skewed or unbounded partition key routes disproportionate traffic to one replica set and bloats SSTable compaction.

Mastering NoSQL at scale means: (1) bounding partition sizes with time buckets (`tenant_id:YYYY-MM-DD`), (2) understanding LSM-Tree write amplification, Bloom filters, and compaction strategies (STCS vs. LCS vs. TWCS), (3) avoiding tombstone storms from TTL deletes and `null` overwrites, and (4) tuning `R + W > N` quorums with hinted handoff and Merkle-tree anti-entropy repair.

domain.purpose: Design, partition, and tune Key-Value, Document, and Wide-Column NoSQL clusters for predictable tail latency, LSM compaction stability, and tunable quorum consistency.

prerequisites.title: Consistent Hashing & Partition Key Routing
prerequisites.summary: A hash ring maps partition keys directly to replica sets in O(1), meaning every read/write must supply the exact partition key to avoid scatter-gather cluster scans.

prerequisites.title: LSM-Tree Write Path (Commit Log + MemTable + SSTables)
prerequisites.summary: Writes append sequentially to an on-disk commit log and sorted in-memory MemTable, flushing immutable SSTables that merge asynchronously via background compaction.

learningJourney.eyebrow: STAGE 01 · SHIFT IN MINDSET & PARTITION KEYS
learningJourney.title: Query-Driven Modeling, Composite Keys & Time-Bucketed Partitions
learningJourney.purpose: Design bounded partition and clustering keys that prevent single-node hot spots and scatter-gather scans.

explanation.foundation: In SQL, you design normalized entity tables first and write arbitrary `WHERE` and `JOIN` clauses later. In NoSQL, **you start with your exact read queries** and shape `(partition_key, clustering_key)` so each query reads a contiguous slice from a single partition.
explanation.core: **The Unbounded Partition Trap**: Partitioning an IoT or audit log table solely by `tenant_id` means an enterprise tenant generating 5M events/day accumulates 1.8 billion rows in one physical partition—exceeding the ~100 MB partition sweet spot and crashing compaction/repair. Adding a time bucket (`PRIMARY KEY ((tenant_id, bucket_date), event_ts, event_id)`) caps every physical partition cleanly and aligns with Time-Window Compaction (TWCS).
explanation.deepDive: **Write Sharding Hot Keys**: When a viral celebrity or flash-sale item hammers one partition key (`item_id = 'concert_99'`), append a bounded random suffix (`concert_99:0..15`) on writes and fan-in 16 parallel reads on reads to distribute write IOPS 16x. learningJourney.title: MemTables, SSTables, Bloom Filters & Compaction Strategies
learningJourney.purpose: Control read amplification and disk I/O spikes by matching compaction strategies to workload patterns.

explanation.foundation: Because SSTables are immutable, updating or deleting a key writes a newer version (or tombstone marker) to a new SSTable. A point read must check the MemTable and potentially multiple SSTables unless accelerated by **in-memory Bloom filters** (which rule out non-existent keys in O(k) hashes with ~1% false-positive rate) and block-offset sparse indexes.
explanation.core:
Choose compaction strategy by workload:
- **Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS)**: Merges similarly sized SSTables; best for pure write-heavy ingest, but requires 50% free disk headroom for major compactions.
- **Leveled Compaction (LCS)**: Organizes SSTables into exponentially growing levels (`L0, L1, L2...`) with non-overlapping key ranges per level; bounds read amplification to 1 SSTable per level (ideal for update-heavy, read-sensitive KV workloads) at higher write amplification.
- **Time-Window Compaction (TWCS)**: Groups SSTables strictly by time window (`1 day`); ideal for TTL time-series because expired windows drop whole files instantly without tombstone compaction.
explanation.deepDive: **Compaction I/O Throttling**: Unthrottled background compaction saturates NVMe read/write bandwidth and spikes p99 read latency; cap compaction throughput (`compaction_throughput_mb_per_sec`) and isolate CPU shards (as ScyllaDB does with thread-per-core shared-nothing architecture).

learningJourney.title: Tunable Quorums (R + W > N), Read Repair & Tombstone Storms
learningJourney.purpose: Configure quorum overlap for strong consistency and eliminate query timeouts caused by delete tombstones.

explanation.foundation: With replication factor $N = 3$, configuring $W = 2$ (LOCAL_QUORUM) and $R = 2$ ensures $R + W = 4 > 3$, guaranteeing at least one replica in every read quorum holds the latest acknowledged write.
explanation.core: **The Tombstone Trap**: In LSM-tree stores, `DELETE` or overwriting columns with `null` does not erase bytes immediately—it writes a **tombstone** marker so offline replicas learn of the deletion during anti-entropy repair instead of resurrecting deleted data (zombie reads). If a queue-like table deletes 500,000 rows in a partition, subsequent `SELECT` scans must read through 500,000 tombstones in memory before finding live rows—triggering `TombstoneOverwhelmingException`.
explanation.deepDive: **Never Use Cassandra/DynamoDB Partitions as FIFO Queues**: Repeatedly inserting and deleting items in the same partition generates massive tombstone piles. Use Kafka or SQS for queues, and rely on TWCS + table-level TTLs for expiring data.

learningJourney.title: Quorum Overlap Verifier & Tombstone-Safe Write Builder in Python
learningJourney.purpose: Enforce quorum invariants and strip null-column tombstones on partial updates in Python.

explanation.foundation: A subtle production bug in Cassandra/DynamoDB drivers is binding `null` for unset optional fields during an `INSERT` or `UPDATE`—every `null` writes an explicit tombstone to disk even when the column was never populated.
explanation.deepDive: Omitting `None` attributes during partial writes eliminates millions of accidental cell-level tombstones across wide-column clusters.

decisionFramework.problem: How to store 90 days of clickstream events (80,000 writes/sec) with automatic expiration and zero tombstone read degradation.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single `user_id` partition key with Leveled Compaction (LCS) and run nightly `DELETE FROM events WHERE ts < cutoff` jobs.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Explicit `DELETE` jobs flood partitions with millions of tombstones, causing read timeouts and heavy compaction I/O.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare explicit `DELETE` jobs with LCS, single-key TTLs with STCS, and time-bucketed partitions `(user_id, YYYY-MM-DD)` with TWCS + row TTL.
decisionFramework.decision: Partition by `(user_id, YYYY-MM-DD)` with Time-Window Compaction Strategy (TWCS) and a 90-day TTL so entire expired daily SSTable files drop cleanly from disk without scanning tombstones.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Eliminates tombstone compaction overhead completely while requiring multi-day queries to issue parallel per-day partition reads.

decisionExercise.prompt: Your ScyllaDB/Cassandra cluster is healthy on CPU and disk space, yet `SELECT` queries on a `user_notifications` table suddenly fail with `TombstoneOverwhelmingException` after reading >100,000 tombstones per query. Investigation reveals a background worker deletes read notifications every hour inside the same `user_id` partition. What fixes this permanently?

options.label: Stop using wide-column partitions as mutable delete-heavy queues; bucket partitions by time with TWCS/TTL or move active notification queues to Redis/SQL.
options.explanation: Correct: LSM-tree stores retain tombstones until `gc_grace_seconds` elapses; high-churn delete queues belong in B+Tree/in-memory stores or time-windowed partitions.

options.label: Set `gc_grace_seconds = 0` across a 3-node cluster so tombstones disappear immediately.
options.explanation: Setting `gc_grace_seconds = 0` before anti-entropy repair runs allows lagging replicas to resurrect deleted notifications (zombie data).

options.label: Increase replication factor from 3 to 5.
options.explanation: Increasing RF replicates the exact same tombstones onto 2 additional nodes without reducing tombstone scans per partition.

learningJourney.eyebrow: STAGE 05 · PRODUCTION BOUNDARIES & WHEN NOT TO USE NOSQL
learningJourney.title: Secondary Index Traps, Cross-Partition Transactions & When SQL Wins
learningJourney.purpose: Identify anti-patterns where NoSQL engines underperform relational or distributed SQL databases.

explanation.foundation: **Global Secondary Index Scatter-Gather Trap**: Querying a low-cardinality secondary index (e.g., `WHERE country = 'IN'`) in a 30-node Cassandra cluster forces the coordinator to scatter-gather across all 30 nodes—destroying p99 latency.
explanation.core:
**When NOT to Use NoSQL**:
- **Complex Ad-Hoc Filtering & Multi-Entity Joins**: Financial ledgers, ERP systems, and CRM apps with dynamic filters belong in PostgreSQL/MySQL.
- **Cross-Partition ACID Invariants**: Double-entry accounting or multi-item inventory checkout across independent partition keys requires relational or Distributed SQL (CockroachDB/Spanner) transactions.
- **Modest Scale (< 3,000 write TPS, < 1 TB)**: A single replicated PostgreSQL primary is far simpler to operate and query.
explanation.deepDive: **Assumptions & Glossary**: **SSTable**: Sorted String Table (immutable sorted key-value file on disk). **Tombstone**: Deletion marker persisted in LSM engines until `gc_grace_seconds` passes. **TWCS**: Time-Window Compaction Strategy. **Hinted Handoff**: Temporary coordinator buffering of writes destined for an unreachable replica.

decisionFramework.question: How do you guarantee strict quorum overlap on reads and writes with replication factor N?
decisionFramework.reason: Configure `R + W > N` (e.g., `N=3, W=2, R=2`) so read and write replica quorums always intersect on at least one up-to-date node.

decisionFramework.question: How do you prevent unbounded partition growth and tombstone storms on time-ordered event tables?
decisionFramework.reason: Compound the partition key with a time bucket (`(entity_id, YYYY-MM-DD)`) and use Time-Window Compaction (TWCS) with TTLs instead of manual `DELETE` jobs.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a replicated NoSQL cluster with replication factor N = 5, which combination of write quorum (W) and read quorum (R) guarantees overlapping replica sets?

options.feedback: 2 + 2 = 4 <= 5; read and write quorums can be completely disjoint.
Correct: by the pigeonhole principle, any two subsets of size 3 out of 5 replicas must share at least 1 replica.
1 + 4 = 5 is not strictly greater than N = 5, so R and W can miss each other.
R = 1, W = 1 optimizes latency/availability (AP) but allows stale reads.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Strict quorum overlap requires R + W > N.

options.feedback: 2 + 2 = 4 <= 5; read and write quorums can be completely disjoint.
Correct: by the pigeonhole principle, any two subsets of size 3 out of 5 replicas must share at least 1 replica.
1 + 4 = 5 is not strictly greater than N = 5, so R and W can miss each other.
R = 1, W = 1 optimizes latency/availability (AP) but allows stale reads.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Strict quorum overlap requires R + W > N.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why do LSM-tree NoSQL databases write 'tombstones' on DELETE instead of immediately erasing data from disk?

options.text: SSTables on disk are immutable, and tombstones ensure lagging or offline replicas learn of the deletion during repair rather than resurrecting deleted data.
options.feedback: Correct: without tombstones, anti-entropy repair would treat a lagging replica's old copy as missing data and restore it.

options.text: Because disks cannot overwrite sectors on SSDs.
options.feedback: SSDs support block erasure; immutability is an LSM-tree design choice for sequential throughput and distributed anti-entropy.

options.text: To increase Bloom filter false-positive rates.
options.feedback: Tombstones exist for distributed deletion propagation, not Bloom filters.

options.text: Because primary keys cannot be indexed in SSTables.
options.feedback: SSTables maintain sparse primary-key indexes.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Tombstones propagate deletions safely across eventually consistent replicas.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which compaction strategy is best suited for time-series data where every row has a fixed 30-day TTL?

options.text: Time-Window Compaction Strategy (TWCS), which groups SSTables by time bucket and drops expired SSTable files whole without tombstone compaction.
options.feedback: Correct: TWCS avoids rewriting old data and reclaims disk space in O(1) file unlinks once a time window expires.
Disabling compaction causes unbounded SSTable counts and severe read amplification.

options.text: Leveled Compaction (LCS) with manual row-by-row DELETE sweeps.
options.feedback: Manual deletes create tombstone storms and high write amplification.
SSTables reside on disk, not purely in a hash table.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: TWCS aligns physical SSTable boundaries with TTL expiration windows.

knowledgeChecks.question: How can binding `null` for unset optional fields during high-rate `INSERT`s degrade a Cassandra or ScyllaDB cluster?

options.text: Each explicit `null` value writes a cell-level tombstone marker, inflating storage and slowing down subsequent reads.
options.feedback: Correct: omitting unset columns from the INSERT statement prevents unnecessary tombstone creation.
It does not drop the table, but it creates excessive tombstones.

options.text: It forces `R = ALL` on every read query.
options.feedback: Consistency level is unaffected.

options.text: It converts the partition key into a random UUID.
options.feedback: Partition keys remain unchanged.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Strip `None`/`null` values from upsert payloads so unpopulated columns never generate tombstones.

tipsAndTricks: Always bound time-ordered partitions with a time bucket (`(entity_id, YYYY-MM-DD)`) so individual partitions stay under ~100 MB.
Never include unset `null` columns in NoSQL upsert payloads—each `null` writes an unnecessary tombstone.
Avoid querying low-cardinality global secondary indexes in large wide-column clusters; maintain explicit query-shaped tables instead.
domainContent.finalSummary: High-scale NoSQL systems deliver predictable single-digit millisecond latency when schemas follow exact query access patterns: keep physical partitions bounded with time buckets, match LSM compaction (LCS vs. TWCS) to mutation/TTL patterns, eliminate accidental tombstones, and configure `R + W > N` quorums according to consistency needs.

beginner.summary: NoSQL databases organize data around fast lookup keys (like Key-Value, Document, or Wide-Column tables) rather than multi-table SQL joins, allowing data to spread cleanly across many servers.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When designing a NoSQL table, choose a partition key that spreads traffic evenly across servers and matches how your app queries the data.
beginner.byteSummary: Instead of joining several tables together on every read, NoSQL stores related data together under a partition key so one server can return your result immediately.

intermediate.summary: Design bounded `(entity_id, time_bucket)` partition keys, align LSM compaction strategies (LCS vs. TWCS) with read/TTL patterns, prevent tombstone accumulation, and enforce `R + W > N` quorum overlap.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When designing storage tiers on NoSQL engines, model partition and clustering keys directly around bounded high-QPS query paths with composite time buckets so writes append sequentially to LSM MemTables without hot-shard throttling or tombstone scan timeouts.
intermediate.byteSummary: LSM-tree NoSQL engines convert random writes into sequential MemTable/SSTable appends. Keeping partitions bounded under ~100 MB, avoiding delete-heavy queue anti-patterns, and stripping null upserts prevent tombstone storms.

advanced.summary: Control write vs. read amplification across STCS/LCS/TWCS compaction tiers, mitigate celebrity partition skew via bounded key salting, coordinate Merkle-tree anti-entropy repair within `gc_grace_seconds`, and avoid scatter-gather secondary index queries.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When operating multi-node LSM NoSQL clusters at scale, pair time-windowed compaction (TWCS) and bounded key salting with scheduled anti-entropy repair within `gc_grace_seconds` so tail latency stays flat and deleted data never resurrects.
advanced.byteSummary: At extreme ingest rates, compaction I/O saturation and tombstone scan limits dominate tail latency. Tuning compaction throughput, isolating thread-per-core shards, and bounding partition cardinality keep p99 predictable.
